title: Accounts Merge
description: Brute force to optimized: repeated pairwise account merging scans versus Union-Find over emails.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Problem Summary: Given a list of accounts, each formatted as [name, email1, email2, ...], where the same person may have multiple accounts listed (identifiable by sharing at least one common email), merge accounts belonging to the same person, returning one account per actual person with all their emails combined and sorted.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","accounts list, each [name, emails...]"],["Output","Merged accounts, one per actual person, emails sorted"],["Key Insight","Union-Find naturally groups emails that end up connected (directly or indirectly) through shared appearances across accounts"],["Constraints","Up to 1000 accounts"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Merge groups that share ANY common element, possibly transitively\"","Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union): union all emails within the same account together, letting shared emails across DIFFERENT accounts transitively merge entire groups"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

Within a single account listing, all its emails clearly belong to the same person, so UNION them together. If two DIFFERENT account listings share even one common email, Union-Find automatically and transitively merges their entire email groups together (since union operations chain naturally), correctly identifying that they belong to the SAME actual person, even across many accounts.

blocks.title: Analogy: Merging Duplicate Contact Entries That Share Any Phone Number or Email
blocks.text: Picture merging duplicate contact entries in a phonebook where multiple entries might actually be the SAME person, identifiable by sharing at least one phone number or email in common, even if the connection is INDIRECT (entry A shares an email with B, and B shares a different email with C, so A, B, and C are all actually the same person).

blocks.caption: Union emails within the same account; two accounts sharing any email end up in the same group

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example accounts (see input)

Result: [["John","john00@mail.com","john_newyork@mail.com","johnsmith@mail.com"],["Mary","mary@mail.com"],["John","johnnybravo@mail.com"]]. The first two "John" accounts share "johnsmith@mail.com" and merge together; "Mary" and the other "John" (with a different email) stay separate.
5. How Should We Think?

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Every email seen across all accounts becomes a node in a Union-Find structure.

Observation 2: Within a single account, union its FIRST email with every other email in that same account, directly connecting all emails belonging to that one listing.

Observation 3: Since accounts are processed one at a time, if a later account's email was ALSO seen in an earlier account, the union operations naturally chain together, transitively merging the two accounts' entire email groups, even without ever comparing two accounts against each other directly.

Observation 4: After processing every account, group all emails by their Union-Find ROOT; each group represents one actual person's complete, merged set of emails, which gets sorted and prefixed with that person's name (found via any email in the group) to form the final answer.
This leads to Union-Find over emails, grouping by final root after processing all accounts, then sorting each group.
6. Brute Force Solution
Repeatedly scan the entire accounts list, merging any two accounts that share a common email, looping until a full pass produces no further merges.
Why the code is written this way

items: Directly comparing every pair of accounts for shared emails implements the merging definition literally.
This costs O(accounts squared) pairwise comparisons per pass, potentially repeated many times; Union-Find processes each account just once, letting shared emails naturally chain merges together.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(accounts squared times emails per account) or worse, due to repeated pairwise comparisons.
Space: O(total emails) for the groups.
Limitation: Union-Find processes each account exactly once, letting the union operations themselves naturally chain together any transitively connected accounts.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Initialize a Union-Find structure where every DISTINCT email seen becomes its own node, and a map from each email to the account holder's name. For each account, union its first email with every other email in that SAME account. After processing all accounts, group every email by its FINAL root (via find). For each group, sort its emails, and prepend the account holder's name (looked up via any email in the group, since they all share the same person's name) to form one merged account entry.
Use Union-Find over emails, unioning within each account, then group by final root and sort.
9. Optimized Solution
Dry run for the two "John" accounts sharing "johnsmith@mail.com"

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Action"],"rows":[["Account 1: John, johnsmith, john_newyork","union(johnsmith, john_newyork)"],["Account 2: John, johnsmith, john00","union(johnsmith, john00)"],["Result","johnsmith, john_newyork, and john00 all end up in the SAME group, transitively"]]}

blocks.text: Why This Works

Unioning every email within a single account together correctly establishes that they all belong to the same person; because accounts are processed in sequence and any email SHARED between two different accounts triggers a union connecting their respective groups, the Union-Find structure naturally and transitively merges ALL accounts belonging to the same actual person, even across chains of shared emails spanning many accounts, without ever needing explicit pairwise account comparisons.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(total emails times inverse Ackermann function, plus total emails log(total emails) for sorting each group).
Space: O(total emails) for the Union-Find structure.
10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.content: {"headers":["Solution","Time","Space","Interview Recommendation"],"rows":[["Repeated pairwise account merging scans","O(accounts^2 times emails) or worse","O(total emails)","Correct, but far slower."],["Union-Find over emails","O(total emails times inverse Ackermann, plus sorting)","O(total emails)","The expected, efficient solution."]]}

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways
Accounts Merge is a hallmark Union-Find application: merging groups by shared elements (emails), even transitively across many accounts.
Common Mistakes

items: Comparing accounts pairwise directly instead of using Union-Find, missing the natural transitive-merging benefit Union-Find provides for free.
Forgetting to sort each group's emails before constructing the final merged account entry.

blocks.text: Edge Cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["Two people happen to share the same NAME but no emails","They remain SEPARATE merged accounts, since merging is based on shared emails, not names."],["An account with only one email, shared by no one else","Remains its own separate merged account."]]}

blocks.text: Interview Tips
Explicitly stating "union emails within an account; shared emails across accounts transitively chain the unions together" demonstrates the key Union-Find insight clearly.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "merge groups sharing common elements, possibly transitively across many groups", think: Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union).
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would you handle this if accounts also needed to be merged by PHONE NUMBER in addition to email, requiring nodes of two different types?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Number of Provinces and Find if Path Exists in Graph, other classic Union-Find applications.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The repeated pairwise merging brute force costs O(accounts squared times emails) or worse; the Union-Find approach costs effectively linear time plus sorting, the standard efficient solution.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union) over shared elements (emails).
Core Idea: union all emails within each account; shared emails across accounts transitively chain the merges together.
Time: O(accounts squared times emails) or worse for the brute force, effectively linear plus sorting for Union-Find.
Most Important Observation: Union-Find naturally handles TRANSITIVE merging across many accounts without explicit pairwise comparisons.
Interview Difficulty: a very frequently asked, classic medium-level Union-Find problem.
One line memory trick: union emails within an account, group by final root.
